text: Elephants use low-frequency rumbles for communication over long distances; some of this sound lies below ordinary human hearing.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Giant pandas leave scent marks on rocks, ground, and tree trunks. The marks carry social information even when the animals are far apart.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, giant panda fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/giant-panda. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A male orangutan's long call resonates in an enlarged throat sac. It advertises his presence across the forest.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, orangutan fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/orangutan. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Some orangutan vocalizations occur in particular wild populations and are absent in others; the Smithsonian describes these differences as cultural.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, orangutan fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/orangutan. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: During courtship, a male kori bustard inflates its esophagus, displays white underfeathers, and may give a low booming call.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, kori bustard fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/kori-bustard. Consulted 2026-10-13.
